who-we-are.card_text: Meet the family-owned team behind the work.

sections.body:
Our roofing professionals bring decades of hands-on experience to every job. Whether it's a single repair or a full re-roof, we treat your property the way we'd want ours treated, and we stand behind the work.

More than 2,500 projects across the Valley have taught us how Arizona roofs actually fail: underlayment that bakes out under tile, foam roofs that lose their coating, flashing that pulls loose after a monsoon wind, and small leaks that go unnoticed until a ceiling stains.
bullets: Family owned & operated
Serving the Valley since 1993
2,500+ successful projects
Licensed, bonded & insured — ROC #096629
Residential, commercial & multi-family

sections.h2: What family owned means for your project
sections.body:
Being family owned isn't a slogan for us. It means the people running the company have their name on the work, and our reputation in the East Valley depends on every roof we touch. We'd rather fix a small problem honestly than sell a big job you don't need.

It also means you deal with a local office, not a call center. When you phone us, you reach the Gilbert office that schedules the crews, and the people who inspect your roof are the same company that does the work.

Our name is our first value. Integrity shows up in small decisions: telling you a roof has years left when it does, photographing what we find so you can see it yourself, and writing estimates you can actually read.
bullets: Honest recommendations. Repair when repair makes sense, replacement when it doesn't.
Clear communication. You'll know what we found, what we recommend and why.
Work done right. Repairs and replacements completed to manufacturer and code requirements.
Respect for your home. We protect your property and clean up when the job is done.
Follow-through. Every project ends with a quality-control check.

sections.body:
Valley homes and buildings use a wide mix of roof systems, and we work on most of them. That includes concrete and clay tile, asphalt shingles, spray foam roofs and recoats, elastomeric coatings, flat roofs and sloped roofs.

Our services cover repair and maintenance, inspections, tile underlayment replacement, storm and monsoon damage repair and full roof replacement for homes and commercial properties.

sections.h2: Why experience matters on Arizona roofs
sections.body:
Desert heat, intense UV and the monsoon season from June 15 to September 30 are hard on roofing materials. A tile roof can look perfect from the street while the underlayment beneath it has dried out and cracked. A foam roof can seem fine until ponding water and UV wear through the coating.

Knowing where to look comes from years on Valley rooftops. Our experience helps us find the real source of a leak, which is often a few feet away from the stain on your ceiling, and recommend the fix that will hold up through the next summer.

The easiest way to get to know us is to call. Reach the Gilbert office at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

You can also learn more about Integrity Roofing, read what customers say on our reviews page, or see our office and service area.

sections.h2: How to check a roofer's credentials
sections.body:
In Arizona, roofing contractors must hold a license from the Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC). You can search any license number on the ROC's website to confirm it's active and see whether complaints are on file. Our license is ROC #096629.

Beyond the license, ask whether the contractor is bonded and insured, who will actually do the work, and whether you'll get a written estimate that spells out the scope. A good roofer will answer those questions without hesitation.

Roofs in the Valley face a different set of problems than roofs in wetter climates. Summer heat and UV break down underlayment, coatings and sealants. Monsoon storms between June 15 and September 30 bring wind, sudden heavy rain and blowing debris that can lift tiles and shingles.

Because we've worked here for so long, we know how each roof type ages in this climate and what maintenance keeps it watertight. That local experience shapes every recommendation we make. Learn more about the roof types we work on.

From our Gilbert office we serve Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Queen Creek, San Tan Valley, Tempe, Phoenix, Scottsdale, Apache Junction, Ahwatukee, Glendale and Peoria. See our local pages for Gilbert, Mesa and Chandler, or visit our location page for office details.

To schedule an estimate or ask a question, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. You can also learn how estimates work before you call.

sections.h2: Had a good experience? Leave a review
sections.body: Reviews take just a minute and make a big difference for a family business. Tell others what we did, how the project went, and how your roof is holding up.

We don't post hand-picked quotes on this page. Instead, we point you to the independent sites where customers write reviews in their own words. That way you see the full picture, not just the comments a company chooses to show.
bullets: Google: The most common place homeowners leave reviews, shown alongside our business listing and map location.
Facebook: Reviews and recommendations on our Facebook page, where we also share job-site videos.
Yelp: Another independent review site where customers rate and describe local contractors.

sections.h2: What to look for in roofer reviews
sections.body: A star rating tells you something, but the written reviews tell you more. When you read reviews for any roofing contractor, look past the number and pay attention to the details.
bullets: The type of job. A great repair review matters most if you need a repair. Look for reviews that match your project.
Communication. Did the company explain what it found, show photos, and keep the homeowner informed?
Follow-through. Did the crew show up when scheduled, clean up, and finish what was promised?
How problems were handled. Every contractor has an occasional issue. How a company responds says a lot.
Reviews over time. A steady history across several years is more meaningful than a burst of recent reviews.
Owner responses. Thoughtful replies to both praise and complaints show a company that pays attention.

sections.h2: How to tell real reviews from fake ones
sections.body: Fake and paid reviews are a real problem across home services. A few patterns can help you separate genuine feedback from reviews that don't deserve your trust.
bullets: Real reviews usually mention specifics: the roof type, the problem, the neighborhood or the timeline.
Watch for many reviews posted within a few days, especially with similar wording.
Check the reviewer's profile. Accounts with a single review, or dozens of five-star reviews in different cities on the same day, deserve a second look.
Overly generic praise with no details ("Great company, best ever!") is less useful than a balanced account.
Compare the same company across Google, Facebook and Yelp. A consistent picture across sites is a good sign.

sections.body:
If you've had work done by us, the most useful reviews describe your actual experience. Your neighbors want to know what you needed, what we found, how the work went and how the roof has performed since.

You don't need to write much. A few honest sentences about the type of roof, the job and how you were treated help other homeowners far more than a star rating alone. Please share both what went well and anything we could do better.

When you call, have your property address handy and describe what you're seeing. We'll review your project and arrange a visit if one is needed. Learn more about our company or who we are.

faqs: Where can I read Integrity Roofing reviews?
On Google, Facebook and Yelp. Use the links on this page to go straight to each site.
How do I leave a review?
Choose Google, Facebook or Yelp above and follow the prompts. A few sentences about your project is plenty.
Why don't you post testimonials on your website?
We'd rather you read reviews on independent sites where customers write in their own words. It gives you a fuller and more trustworthy picture than a page of selected quotes.
What should I look for in a roofer's reviews?
Look for reviews that match your type of project, mention communication and cleanup, and describe how problems were handled. A steady history over several years matters more than a single rating.
How can I spot fake roofing reviews?
Be cautious of many similar reviews posted in a short window, profiles with only one review, and vague praise with no details. Compare the company across several review sites.
Is one bad review a reason not to hire a roofer?
Not necessarily. Look at how the company responded and whether the issue was resolved. A pattern of the same complaint is more telling than a single negative review.
Do you pay for or offer incentives for reviews?
No. We simply ask customers to share an honest review if they're willing.
What if I had a problem with my project?
Please call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm, so we can make it right. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.
Can I update my review later?
Yes. Google, Facebook and Yelp all let you edit your own review, so you can add how your roof held up after a monsoon season.
Besides reviews, how else can I check a roofer?
Verify the contractor's license with the Arizona Registrar of Contractors, confirm they're bonded and insured, and ask for a written estimate. Our license is ROC #096629.

sections.h2: What we'll ask on the call
sections.body: You don't need to know anything technical about roofing. We'll ask a few simple questions so we can send the right person and plan the visit.
bullets: Your name and a good callback number. So we can confirm your appointment.
The property address. Where the roof is, including the city.

Can you give me a price over the phone?
Not an accurate one. Every roof is different, so we inspect before we price. For typical ranges, see the Roofing Cost Guide on our site.
Do you do estimates for commercial roofs?
Yes. We provide estimates for residential, commercial and multi-family roofs.
Can I schedule an estimate on a weekend?
The office is closed Saturday and Sunday. Call Monday to Friday, or leave a message any time and we'll call you back within 24 hours.

sections.h2: What you'll see in these photos

bullets: Tile roofs: concrete and clay tile, the most common roof on Valley homes.

Other roof types: shingle, foam, coated and flat roofs on homes and commercial buildings.

sections.h2: Why tile underlayment shows up so often
sections.body:
On a tile roof, the tile itself sheds most of the water and shields the layer below from the sun. The underlayment underneath is what actually keeps water out of the home. In Arizona heat, that underlayment dries out, becomes brittle and cracks over time, even while the tiles still look fine from the street.

That's why many tile projects involve lifting the tile, installing new underlayment and resetting the sound tiles. Photos of this work show what's hidden beneath a tile roof. Learn more on our tile roofs page.

sections.h2: Using photos to understand your own roof
sections.body: Project photos can help you put a name to what you're seeing on your own home. Compare the roof type and condition in the gallery with your roof, viewed safely from the ground or with binoculars. Please don't climb onto your roof to check.
bullets: Identify your roof type: tile, shingle, foam, coated or flat.
Notice how a finished roof's lines look: straight rows, even edges and tight ridges.
See what's normally hidden, such as underlayment and flashing, so a contractor's explanation makes sense.
Get a sense of what a repair involves compared with a full re-roof.

sections.h2: Warning signs to look for on your roof
sections.body: Some roof problems are visible from the ground. If you notice any of the following, it may be time for a roof inspection.
bullets: Cracked, broken or slipped tiles, especially after monsoon winds.
Missing, curled or lifted shingles.
Exposed underlayment where tiles have shifted.
Blisters, cracks or bare spots on foam and coated roofs.
Standing water on a flat roof a day or more after rain.
Debris built up in valleys and around roof penetrations.
Water stains on ceilings or walls inside the home.

sections.body:
A photo shows one roof on one day. Your roof's age, materials, pitch and history all affect what it needs. The only way to know for sure is an in-person inspection, where we photograph what we find on your roof and walk you through it.

To schedule an estimate, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. You can also watch our crew at work on the media page.

faqs: Are these photos of real Integrity Roofing projects?
Yes. The gallery shows work completed by our crews on homes and buildings across the Phoenix Valley.
What types of roofs are shown?
Mostly tile roofs, plus shingle, foam, coated and flat roofs, including repairs, underlayment replacement and full re-roofs.
What is tile underlayment?
It's the waterproof layer beneath roof tiles. The tiles protect it from sun and shed most water, but the underlayment is what keeps water out of the home.
Why would tiles be removed if they aren't broken?
When the underlayment under the tile wears out, the tiles are lifted so new underlayment can be installed. Sound tiles are then reset on the roof.
What does a finished re-roof usually look like?
Rows should be straight and even, edges and ridges should be tight and neat, and there should be no debris left behind on the roof or around the home.
How can I tell what kind of roof I have?
Look from the ground. Tile has curved or flat rows of heavy pieces, shingles are flat overlapping strips, and foam or coated roofs are usually smooth, seamless surfaces on low-slope roofs.
Can photos tell me if my roof needs replacing?
They can help you recognize warning signs, but not diagnose your roof. An in-person inspection is the only reliable way to know.
Should I go on my roof to compare it with these photos?
No. Stay on the ground and use binoculars or look from a window. Walking on a roof is risky and can crack tiles.
Will you photograph my roof during an estimate?
Yes. We photograph what we find during the inspection so you can see the conditions yourself.
Do you have videos as well?
Yes. Our media page has job-site videos and short tips from our team.

Yes. The projects shown come from across our service area, which includes Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Queen Creek, San Tan Valley, Tempe, Phoenix, Scottsdale, Apache Junction, Ahwatukee, Glendale and Peoria.

Call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

sections.h2: Why roof leaks are hard to find
sections.body:
The spot where water shows up on your ceiling is often not where it enters the roof. Water can travel along underlayment, decking or framing before it drips through. On tile roofs, the source is usually a worn spot in the underlayment or a problem at a valley, flashing or penetration.

That's why a good leak repair starts with tracing the water's path, not just patching the area above the stain. Learn more about roof repair and maintenance.

sections.h2: What to watch for in roofing videos
sections.body: Watching a crew at work can help you understand what goes into a quality job, and what to ask any roofer you're considering.
bullets: Safety practices on the roof.
Care taken with tiles that are being lifted and reset.
Attention to valleys, edges, flashing and penetrations, where leaks usually begin.
How underlayment is laid and overlapped on tile roofs.
Cleanup of debris and old materials.

sections.body:
Videos are a helpful way to see things you'd never see from the ground. Once you've watched how a tile roof is built in layers, it's easier to understand why a roof that looks fine from the street can still leak, and why an inspection looks beneath the surface.

For more photos, see our project gallery. For written guides, visit the resource center or browse quick answers on our FAQ page.

Many of the problems you'll see in roofing videos come from Arizona's climate. Long summers of heat and UV wear down underlayment, sealants and coatings. The monsoon season, from June 15 to September 30, adds wind, heavy rain and blowing debris.

The best time to have a roof checked is before monsoon season starts, so small problems can be fixed before the storms arrive. After a strong storm, look for slipped tiles, missing shingles or debris on the roof from the ground, and call if you notice anything.

faqs: Are these videos of real Integrity Roofing jobs?
Yes. The job-site videos show our crews at work on roofs around the Phoenix Valley.
Where can I see more videos?
Our Facebook page has more job-site videos. Several are linked on this page.
Why doesn't the leak show up where the water enters?
Water often travels along underlayment, decking or framing before it drips through the ceiling, so the entry point can be several feet away from the stain.
What is the most common cause of leaks on tile roofs?
Worn underlayment beneath the tile is a frequent cause in Arizona, along with problems at valleys, flashing and roof penetrations.
Can I fix a roof leak myself after watching a video?
We don't recommend it. Roof work is dangerous, and walking on tile can crack it. A professional repair also finds the true source of the leak.
When is the best time to have my roof checked?
Before monsoon season starts on June 15 is ideal, so small problems can be repaired before the storms. After a strong storm is also a good time.
What should I look for after a monsoon storm?
From the ground, look for slipped or broken tiles, missing shingles, loose flashing and debris on the roof. Inside, check ceilings for new stains.
Do you have photos of your work too?
Yes. Our gallery page has photos of tile, shingle, foam and flat roofing projects.
Why is underlayment so important on a tile roof?

The tile sheds most of the water and shades the layer below, but the underlayment is the true waterproof barrier. When it dries out and cracks in Arizona heat, leaks follow even if the tiles look fine.

sections.h2: Roofing advice written for the desert
sections.body:
Most roofing advice online is written for places with snow, ice and constant rain. Arizona roofs face something different: months of intense heat and UV, followed by a monsoon season from June 15 to September 30 that brings wind, sudden downpours and blowing debris.

Our tips come from more than 30 years of work on Valley roofs. They're meant to help you understand your roof, spot problems early, and make good decisions when it's time for a repair or replacement.

A little attention each year helps a roof last longer. Our maintenance tips cover what to check from the ground, how to keep valleys and drains clear, and why coatings on foam and flat roofs need periodic renewal.
bullets: Look over your roof from the ground in spring and after major storms.
Keep debris out of valleys, gutters and roof drains.
Watch ceilings and walls for new stains.
Plan foam and coated roof recoats before the coating wears through.

sections.body: The weeks before June 15 are the best time to get a roof ready for storm season. We write about what to check, how wind lifts tiles and shingles, and what to do after a storm. If your roof is damaged, see our page on storm and monsoon damage repair.

Many questions we hear come down to one decision: repair or replace? Our articles explain how tile underlayment ages, what an inspection looks for, and the signs that a roof is near the end of its life. Learn more about roof inspections, repairs and roof replacement.

Valley homes use several roof systems, and each ages differently. Tile roofs depend on the underlayment beneath them, shingles wear from heat and UV, and foam and coated roofs need regular recoating. Our roof types page explains the differences, with more detail on tile, shingles, foam and flat roofs.

For in-depth guides, visit our resource center. It brings together longer articles on roof types, costs and planning a project, including the Roofing Cost Guide with typical price ranges. Every roof is different, so use the guide as a starting point.

The roofing library is where to look up terms and topics, from underlayment and flashing to elastomeric coatings and spray foam. It's useful when a contractor uses a word you don't recognize or you want to understand what's on your estimate.
Sign up for our newsletter for seasonal reminders, such as pre-monsoon checks and summer heat tips, plus new articles as we publish them.

Short on time? Our FAQ page answers the most common questions about roofs, estimates, financing and scheduling. If you don't see your question, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: Who writes these roofing tips?
They come from Integrity Roofing, a family-owned roofing contractor in Gilbert, AZ that has worked on Valley roofs since 1993.
Is this advice specific to Arizona?
Yes. Our tips focus on how heat, UV and monsoon storms affect roofs in the Phoenix Valley.
When does monsoon season start in Arizona?
Monsoon season runs from June 15 to September 30. The weeks before it starts are a good time to have your roof checked.
Where can I find in-depth roofing guides?
Visit our resource center at /resources/ for longer guides on roof types, costs and planning a project.
What is the roofing library?
It's a collection of roofing terms and topics that helps you understand words like underlayment, flashing and elastomeric coating.
How much does a new roof cost in Arizona?
It depends on the roof type, size, pitch and condition. Our Roofing Cost Guide lists typical ranges, but every roof is different and an estimate is the only way to know.
How can I get new tips as they're published?
Sign up for our newsletter for seasonal reminders and new articles.
How often should I check my roof?
Look it over from the ground at least once a year, ideally before monsoon season, and again after any strong storm.
Why do tile roofs leak if the tiles look fine?
The underlayment under the tile is what keeps water out. Heat and UV dry it out over time, so it can crack and leak even when the tiles look perfect from the street.
Can I ask a roofing question that isn't covered here?
